answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: Born 1930 · American investor; chairman of Berkshire Hathaway
answer.sourceLine: Credibly and very widely credited to Buffett, and entirely in character — but the wording reaches us through a single listener. Todd Combs recalled it from a Columbia Business School investing class, and Quote Investigator ↗ finds its earliest printing in a 2013 Omaha World-Herald profile, with no contemporaneous transcript or recording behind it.

source.excerpt: Read 500 pages like this every day. That’s how knowledge works. It builds up, like compound interest. All of you can do it, but I guarantee not many of you will do it.
source.trailTitle: How a classroom aside became an internet commandment
trail: Circa 2002 — a classroom, no recorder running. Todd Combs, who took his MBA at Columbia Business School in 2002 (Wikipedia ↗), hears Buffett answer a student question about preparing for an investing career. Nothing is published at the time.

2010 — the first printed page-count is weekly, and it is about Combs. When the Wall Street Journal reports Buffett tapping Combs, it describes Combs as reading 500 pages a week; Quote Investigator ↗ notes this citation does not contain the famous sentence at all.

28 April 2013 — the sentence appears in print. Steve Jordon’s Omaha World-Herald profile of Berkshire’s investment managers carries Combs’s recollection; QI identifies this as the first citation printing the exact words ↗.

Afterwards — the “a day” version takes over. Business media recycle it relentlessly, while at least one investing columnist argues Buffett actually said 500 pages a week (GuruFocus via Yahoo Finance ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is the wording as it entered print in 2013, reconstructed from memory by a student who heard it roughly a decade earlier. Treat the sentence structure as reported speech rather than a transcript.
source.rightsHolder: Omaha World-Herald (Steve Jordon), for the 2013 article in which the wording first appeared
source.rightsNote: There is no pre-1931 work here to fall back on: the remark was spoken circa 2002 and first fixed in print in a 2013 newspaper article, so both the article and the reported wording are modern, in-copyright material. Quotle.info reproduces the sentence as short quotation for identification and fact-checking, not as a public-domain text.

author.bio: Warren Buffett, born 30 August 1930, built Berkshire Hathaway from a failing textile firm into one of the world’s largest conglomerates and became the most quoted investor alive. His public voice is unusually well documented — decades of annual shareholder letters and marathon meeting Q&As — which is part of why an undocumented Buffett line stands out. He handed the chief executive role to Greg Abel on 1 January 2026 and remained chairman.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong about this one
misattribution.intro: Nobody serious claims a different author — the problem is precision. The line is quoted as though someone wrote it down at the time, and the page count itself is contested.

items.who: “500 pages a day” vs “500 pages a week”
items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ records that the 2010 Wall Street Journal piece used the weekly figure, and a 2018 GuruFocus column by Adam Parris argues outright that Buffett said 500 pages a week ↗. Even Farnam Street’s much-shared write-up of the Combs story renders the advice as weekly ↗.

items.who: A transcript that does not exist
items.why: There is no known recording, transcript or contemporaneous note of the class. QI ↗ calls the evidence substantive but flags the significant delay before publication and leaves open that an earlier citation may be found.
The line does not appear on Wikiquote’s Warren Buffett page ↗, whose sourced sections draw mainly on his shareholder letters and meeting remarks.

The remark is advice Buffett is remembered giving to students, but it circulates as a statistic about Buffett’s personal habits. The 600-to-1,000-pages-a-day figure that often travels with it belongs to Combs, not Buffett, in the Omaha World-Herald account (quoted here ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Best available reading: Buffett very likely said something close to this in a Columbia classroom, but every printed version descends from one student’s memory published in 2013 — so quote it as attributed, and do not present the daily page count as settled fact (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why this line travels so well
lead: Compounding is Buffett’s native metaphor — it is the mechanism his entire career is built on — so hearing him apply it to reading feels less like a quotation and more like a signature. That is exactly what makes it hard to police: the sentence is so characteristic that few people who repeat it ever think to ask where it was written down.

The answer is that it was not written down, at least not for years. It surfaced in an Omaha World-Herald profile of the two investment managers Buffett had recruited, where Todd Combs described taking the advice literally and building a reading habit around it. The anecdote is the reason we have the sentence at all — and it is also the reason the wording cannot be checked against anything.
detailsBody: The day-versus-week wobble is worth sitting with. The earliest printed page count in this whole story is weekly, and it describes Combs rather than Buffett; the daily version only arrives with Combs’s 2013 recollection. Quote Investigator lays both out side by side without declaring a winner, and a page that is honest about its sources should do the same.
None of this makes the advice wrong. It makes the quotation marks a claim — and a claim resting on one memory, published long after the fact, is an attribution rather than a verified text.
context.pull: It sounds exactly like Buffett. That is precisely why it needs a source rather than a vibe.
